## Question And Audience

**Audience:** Public health program managers who are not data specialists, receiving a short equity briefing on middle-income adults.

**Question:** How did average body mass index (BMI) among middle-income adults aged 20 to 80 differ across NHANES survey waves in the classroom dataset?

**Why it matters:** Program managers need a clear picture of what this data does and does not show before deciding whether to look into it further.

## Evidence

![Source: prepared classroom snapshot derived from CDC/NCHS NHANES public-use data [@cdc-nhanes]. Results are descriptive and unweighted.](../../assignment07-dashboard/submission/dashboard-preview.png){.r-stretch}

## Takeaway

In this classroom dataset, middle-income adults surveyed in 2021-2023 had a higher average BMI (30.3) than those surveyed in 1999-2000 (29.0).

## Limitation And Next Step {.smaller}

**Limitation:** This unweighted, descriptive summary does not give national estimates or show why average BMI differed between survey waves. Each survey wave included different people, so it does not follow the same adults over time. The graph's y-axis does not start at 0, so the change can look bigger than it is.

**Next step:** Before using these results in planning, ask for an analysis that uses the NHANES survey weights, which adjust for how people were chosen for the survey, so the averages can represent US adults.
